column2: Too much sugar and salt is linked to heart disease, tooth decay and weight problems.
Added sugar should be less than 10% (ideally 5%) of daily energy.
No added sugar is recommended under 2 years.
Ready-made foods are the biggest source of hidden sugar and salt.
Check labels for words like "sugar, glucose syrup, fructose".
Use spices and lemon instead of salt in cooking.
Satisfy sweet cravings with fruit.
Vegetarian and vegan eating
Well-planned plant-based eating is possible at any age; some nutrients need attention.
Vitamin B12 isn't found in plant foods; vegans need a supplement.
Iron, zinc, iodine, calcium and omega-3 need careful planning.
A vegan diet in pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy should be planned with a specialist.
Eat legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds every day.
Ask your doctor or a dietitian about B12 and other supplements.
Tiredness, numbness or tingling, paleness; poor growth in children.
Preterm birth and premature babies
Birth before week 37 of pregnancy is called preterm birth.
Signs: regular contractions, lower back pain, pressure in the pelvis, change in discharge, leaking fluid.
Development in premature babies is assessed by corrected age.
Breast milk is especially valuable for premature babies.
With signs of preterm labour, go to hospital without delay.
Don't miss check-ups and eye and hearing screenings for a premature baby.
Do skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) in the neonatal unit if possible.
Regular contractions, leaking fluid or bleeding before week 37.
Recovery after a caesarean
A caesarean is major abdominal surgery; recovery usually takes 6–8 weeks.
Moving early in the first days reduces the risk of clots.
It is recommended not to lift anything heavier than your baby and to wait for your doctor's OK before driving.
Breastfeeding after a caesarean is possible; side-lying or the rugby-ball hold can be comfortable.
Take painkillers regularly; don't let pain stop you moving.
Keep the wound clean and dry.
Support your tummy with a pillow when coughing or laughing.
Redness, discharge or opening of the wound; fever.
Swelling and pain in the leg, shortness of breath: emergency.
Birth plan and preparation
A birth plan is a short note that helps you share your birth preferences with the team.
A birth plan should be flexible; the medical situation may change.
Support person, pain relief, skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding preferences are common topics.
Write your preferences on no more than 1 page and discuss them with your doctor.
Find out your hospital's labour ward rules in advance.
Practise breathing and relaxation techniques before the birth.
Anxiety and emotional changes in pregnancy
Pregnancy can bring worry as well as excitement; mood swings are normal.
Hormonal changes, tiredness and uncertainty can affect your mood.
Depression can also occur in pregnancy and can be treated.
Share your worries with your partner, family or midwife.
Antenatal classes can reduce uncertainty.
Regular movement, sleep and a balanced diet support your mood.
Unhappiness, hopelessness or sleeplessness lasting more than two weeks.
Thoughts of harming yourself: call your local emergency number right away.
Parental burnout
Long-term exhaustion, emotional distance from your child and a sense of inadequacy can be signs of parental burnout.
Burnout doesn't mean you're a bad parent; it's a sign you need support.
Perfectionism and not asking for help increase the risk.
Share responsibilities; try saying "no".
Give yourself a short break every day.
Consider talking to a mental health professional.
Struggling to control anger towards your child, thoughts of harming yourself: get support right away.
Pregnancy loss and grief
People who experience pregnancy loss may grieve deeply; getting support during this time is important.
Most early pregnancy losses are not caused by anything the mother did.
Grief varies from person to person; partners may grieve differently.
Talk to people you can share your feelings with.
Go to your check-ups for physical recovery.
Ask for help from a professional or support groups.
Heavy bleeding, fever or tummy pain.
Grief and hopelessness that affect daily life for a long time.
Mother's sleep
Good sleep is the basis of mental health; with a baby you need a plan to protect it.
Even short naps reduce tiredness.
Sleep deprivation can increase symptoms of anxiety and depression.
Consider expressed milk or formula so night feeds can be shared.
Put your phone away before bed; keep the bedroom dark and cool.
Cut down on caffeine in the afternoon.
Maternity leave and working mothers' rights
Maternity leave, breastfeeding breaks and part-time working rights are set by law and differ from country to country.
In Türkiye, the Labour Law gives a total of 16 weeks of paid maternity leave before and after birth (18 weeks for multiple pregnancies).
In Türkiye, there is a daily breastfeeding break until the child turns one.
Details vary by public or private sector, type of work and current regulations.
Check your rights with your HR department and official sources in your country.
Keep leave and medical certificate dates in the app's family calendar.
Your baby's official paperwork
After birth, civil registration and health cover procedures need to be done on time.
The birth must be registered within the legal deadline; hospitals often notify the birth electronically.
Registering your baby with a family doctor is needed for vaccinations and check-ups.
Complete the birth registration and identity document procedures.
Check the family doctor registration and health cover notification.
Check current conditions for any support such as birth grants from official sources.
Grandparents and family support
The wider family is an important source of support; shared rules reduce conflict.
Advice on safe sleep, honey, sugar and screens has changed over time.
Consistent rules help a child feel safe.
Share important rules (sleep, feeding, medicine) in writing.
Thank them for their help; talk about boundaries kindly but clearly.
Home organisation and time management with a baby
Simple systems and small habits make life with a baby easier.
You can't do everything at once; setting priorities reduces stress.
Gather nappy-changing and feeding supplies in 1–2 spots at home.
Plan the weekly menu and shopping list in the app.
Batch-cook meals and freeze them in portions.
Pick 3 important tasks for the day; keep the rest flexible.
Pregnancy weeks are counted from the first day of your last period; this week is actually your period and you are not yet pregnant.
You're on your period. Your body is preparing for a new ovulation.
If you're planning a pregnancy, start folic acid; stop alcohol and smoking.
Ovulation usually happens towards the end of this week; fertilisation can occur within about a day after ovulation.
Around ovulation there may be clear, slippery discharge and mild pelvic pain.
You can follow your fertile days in the app's cycle calendar.
The fertilised egg (zygote) divides quickly as it travels towards the womb.
Most women don't feel anything yet.
Ask your doctor about the medicines you take in case you are pregnant.
The cluster of cells implants in the womb wall; the pregnancy hormone (hCG) starts to rise.
A late period, mild cramps or light spotting may occur. A home pregnancy test may be positive.
If the test is positive, book a doctor's appointment; keep taking folic acid.
The foundations of the heart and nervous system form; the neural tube starts to close.
Tiredness, breast tenderness and frequent weeing may begin.
At your first visit, review your chronic conditions and medicines.
The heartbeat can be seen on ultrasound; arm and leg buds appear.
Nausea may start; sensitivity to smells may increase.
Limit caffeine to 200 mg a day; eat small amounts often.
The brain develops quickly; facial features start to form.
Nausea, mood swings and tiredness are common.
The first ultrasound confirms the week of pregnancy; enter your due date in the app.
about 1.6 cm · 1 g
Fingers start to become distinct; the embryo makes small movements that can't be felt yet.
Bloating and tiredness may continue.
First tests such as blood group, blood count and infection screening are done.
about 2.3 cm · 2 g
Most of the major organs have formed; the eyelids develop.
Nausea may be at its worst in these weeks.
For nausea, try not to go hungry; if you can't keep anything down, see your doctor.
about 3.1 cm · 4 g
The embryo stage ends and the "foetus" stage begins; the vital organs are in place.
Blood volume increases; veins may look more visible.
Discuss screening options (combined test, cell-free DNA test) with your doctor.
about 4.1 cm · 7 g
The head is about half the body length; nail beds and tooth buds develop.
Nausea may start to ease; you may feel dizzy when standing up quickly.
Plan your appointment for the screening test between weeks 11 and 14.
about 5.4 cm · 14 g
Reflexes develop; your baby can open and close their fingers. The kidneys start producing urine.
The womb rises above the pelvic bone; frequent weeing may ease a little.
Nuchal translucency measurement and the combined test can be done now.
about 7.4 cm · 23 g
The vocal cords develop; the intestines settle into place in the abdomen.
Many pregnant women start to feel more energetic.
Have a dental check-up; gums can become sensitive in pregnancy.
about 8.7 cm · 43 g
Facial expressions may begin; the body starts to be covered in fine hair (lanugo).
Appetite increases; your bump starts to show.
Build an exercise routine such as regular walks.
about 10 cm · 70 g
Bones continue to harden; although the eyelids are closed, sensitivity to light develops.
A blocked nose and bleeding gums may occur.
Ask your doctor whether you need iron supplements.
about 11.6 cm · 100 g
Muscles and skeleton get stronger; the head is held more upright.
Darkening of the skin (pregnancy mask) and a line down the middle of the tummy may appear.
If your doctor recommends it, the triple/quadruple screening test is done in weeks 15–20.
about 13 cm · 140 g
Fat starts to build up under the skin; sweat glands develop.
Your centre of gravity shifts; back pain may start.
Wear comfortable shoes and a supportive bra.
about 14 cm · 190 g
The ears move into position and may start to pick up sounds.
You may feel the first movements like "butterfly wings" (especially in later pregnancies).
Plan your detailed ultrasound appointment.
about 15 cm · 240 g
A protective white coating (vernix) starts to cover the skin.
Brief, sharp pains at the sides of the bump (round ligament pain) may occur.
Start pelvic floor exercises.
about 25 cm (head to heel) · 300 g
You're halfway through. Your baby makes swallowing movements; movements become clearer.
Your bump becomes more obvious; your belly button may flatten.
The detailed (anomaly) scan is usually done in weeks 18–22.
about 27 cm · 360 g
The digestive system develops; it starts processing the amniotic fluid swallowed.
Leg cramps and varicose veins may appear.
Look into antenatal classes.
about 28 cm · 430 g
The senses develop; your baby can feel touch and eyebrows appear.
Stretch marks may appear on the tummy, hips and breasts.
Prepare a baby budget and needs list in the app's shopping section.
about 29 cm · 500 g
Blood vessels develop in the lungs; rhythmic jolts (hiccups) may be felt.
There may be mild swelling at the ankles.
Start getting to know your baby's movement pattern.
about 30 cm · 600 g
The lungs start producing a substance that reduces surface tension (surfactant).
Heartburn may become more frequent.
Gestational diabetes screening (glucose tolerance test) is done in weeks 24–28.
about 34 cm · 660 g
The grasp reflex develops; hair grows longer.
Trouble sleeping may start.
Plan the nursery and a safe sleep space.
about 35 cm · 760 g
The eyes start to open; your baby may react to sounds.
Mild swelling and irregular, painless tightenings (false contractions) may occur.
Get used to sleeping on your left side.
about 36 cm · 875 g
Sleep–wake cycles become regular; brain activity increases.
You may feel short of breath.
If your blood group is Rh negative, discuss what is needed around week 28 with your doctor.
about 38 cm · 1 kg
The eyes can open and close. The third trimester begins.
Tiredness may return; you may get restless legs.
Track movements every day; a blood count may be repeated.
about 39 cm · 1.2 kg
Muscles and lungs mature; kicks get stronger.
Constipation and haemorrhoids may occur.
Learn about breastfeeding; you can start with the guide in the app.
about 40 cm · 1.3 kg
The brain grows fast; bone marrow produces blood cells.
Trouble sleeping and mood swings may increase.
Start writing your birth preferences (birth plan).
about 41 cm · 1.5 kg
Sensory perception develops; your baby gains weight fast.
A yellowish fluid (colostrum) may come from the breasts.
Confirm the hospital where you'll give birth and how you'll get there.
about 42 cm · 1.7 kg
Nails grow, fine hair starts to shed; most babies turn head down.
False contractions may become more frequent.
An ultrasound may be done to check growth.
about 44 cm · 1.9 kg
Bones harden (the skull stays flexible); more antibodies pass from mother to baby.
There may be pain in the back, hips and wrists.
Buy a rear-facing car seat and learn how to fit it.
about 45 cm · 2.1 kg
The central nervous system and lungs continue to mature.
Tiredness and frequent weeing increase.
Pack your hospital bag.
about 46 cm · 2.4 kg
The kidneys finish developing; the liver's function increases.
The womb rises up to the ribs; you may feel short of breath.
Have the last-month tests your doctor recommends.
about 47 cm · 2.6 kg
Fat keeps building up; your baby may start to drop into the pelvis.
When your baby drops, breathing gets easier but you'll wee more often.
Check-ups become more frequent; have your bag and documents ready.
about 49 cm · 2.9 kg
Organs keep maturing (early term).
A show (bloody mucus) may come; pressure in the pelvis increases.
Review the signs of labour and when to go to hospital.
about 50 cm · 3.1 kg
The grip is strong; reactions to sound and light are clear.
You may feel swollen and impatient.
Prioritise rest; keep tracking movements.
about 51 cm · 3.3 kg
Full term. Brain and lung development continues.
Try to tell irregular and regular contractions apart.
Go to the monitoring check-ups your doctor recommends (e.g. NST).
about 51 cm · 3.4 kg
Due week. Only a small share of babies are born exactly on this date.
The wait can cause anxiety; rest and ask for support.
If labour doesn't start, find out your doctor's monitoring plan; an assessment is usually done at 41 weeks.
Bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, vomiting so much you can't keep anything down, fever: get checked without delay.
Bleeding, leaking fluid, regular painful contractions, severe headache, vision problems, sudden swelling of the face and hands: get checked without delay.
A clear decrease in baby's movements, bleeding, leaking fluid, regular contractions, severe headache or vision problems: get checked the same day. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.
Newborns see faces best from 20–30 cm away and recognise their mother's voice and smell. They have sucking, grasping and startle reflexes.
Skin-to-skin contact, face-to-face talking, lullabies. Brief supervised tummy time while awake.
Tries to lift the head briefly; hands are in fists. Startles or calms at sounds. Briefly follows a nearby face with the eyes.
Black-and-white contrast cards, slowly moving your face side to side for them to follow, tummy play a few times a day.
The social smile begins; makes sounds like "agoo". Can lift the head 45° on the tummy and starts to open the hands.
Smile back at their smile, imitate their sounds. Gently shake a rattle and wait for them to find the sound.
Holds the head more upright; brings the hands together and to the mouth. Almost-laughs, looks at colourful objects for longer.
Reaching for toys hung at chest level, mirror play, gentle leg cycling.
Holds the head upright and steady; reaches for and holds objects. Laughs, pushes up on the arms when on the tummy. Attempts at rolling may begin.
Safe toys within reach, different textures, sound books. When talking, pause and wait for them to "answer".
Rolls over (usually tummy to back); puts objects in the mouth. Starts responding to their name, tells tones of voice apart.
Free movement on a safe floor mat, placing a toy a little away to encourage reaching, songs with hand games.
Sits with support; passes an object from one hand to the other. May try syllables like "ba" and "ma". Recognises familiar faces.
A cushion for sitting support, putting objects in and out of a container, peekaboo, thick picture books.
Can sit briefly without support; turns towards where a sound comes from. Babbling increases; shows interest in their mirror image.
Toys to hold with both hands, banging things together (rhythm), facial expressions in the mirror.
Sits without support, gets ready to crawl or creeps. Stranger anxiety may begin. Object permanence develops: looks for a hidden object.
Finding a toy hidden under a cloth, a tunnel/cushion course that encourages crawling (supervised), "all gone" game.
Crawls; tries to pull up to stand. Starts picking up small objects with thumb and forefinger. Syllables like "baba", "mama".
Soft blocks, boxes with lids, waving and clapping games. Keep talking through daily tasks.
Pulls up on furniture and may cruise sideways. Understands simple words ("no", "come"); waves.
Push toys (sturdy, won't tip over), rolling a ball, imitating animal sounds.
Walks holding on; can stand alone briefly. Points to ask for things, starts understanding simple instructions.
